issues.legal_issue: A congenitally disqualified member of a Mitakshara joint family retains an interest in ancestral coparcenary property sufficient to take the whole estate by survivorship when he becomes the sole surviving member.
material_facts: The disputed property was ancestral joint-family property.
The deceased father left a son who had been deaf and mute from birth, and the disability disqualified him from inheriting under the law then applicable.
The son survived his father without another qualified male coparcener remaining; the son later died leaving a widow and daughter.
The succession arose before the statutory removal of the relevant disqualification applied.
issues.conclusion: The disqualified son was not to be treated as if he did not exist: he could take and enjoy the whole estate as the sole surviving coparcener, and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Hindu law applicable to the succession, the Mitakshara (Chapter II, Section 10, including placita 1, 5, 6 and 9) excluded a disqualified heir from participation or enjoyment while preserving maintenance and the rights of his qualified issue. The Sarasvati Vilasa (placita 148–159) distinguished a share-taker from a share-enjoyer; the Court treated that work as an authority in Southern India and found no contrary Mitakshara text. The Court relied on Krishna v. Sami, ILR 9 Mad 64 (FB); Muthusami Gurukkal v. Meenammal, ILR 48 Mad 464; Amirthammal v. Vallimayil Ammal, ILR 1942 Mad 807 (FB); Kesava v. Govindan, ILR 1946 Mad 452 (FB); and the approval of related principles in Kumari Ratnesvari v. Bhagwati Saran Singh, 1949 FCR 715. Section 2 of the Hindu Inheritance (Removal of Disabilities) Act, 1928 removed the disqualification prospectively, while section 3 preserved previously accrued rights and liabilities; the Act therefore did not govern this succession.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_inheritance and ancestral_joint_family_property and congenitally_disqualified_member and marriage_capable_member and member_outlived_other_coparceners and no_other_coparcener_remained and pre_statutory_succession_event

predicates.appeal_concerning_inheritance: The proceeding is an appeal concerning competing claims to inherit joint-family property.
predicates.ancestral_joint_family_property: The property in dispute was ancestral property held by a joint family.
predicates.congenitally_disqualified_member: A member of the family had a congenital condition that disqualified him from inheritance under the applicable law.
predicates.marriage_capable_member: The disqualified member was capable of marriage.
predicates.member_outlived_other_coparceners: The disqualified member survived the other relevant coparceners.
predicates.no_other_coparcener_remained: No other coparcener remained when the disqualified member was the surviving member of the family.
predicates.pre_statutory_succession_event: The succession arose before the statutory change removing the relevant disqualification applied.

issues.definition: When an inheritance appeal concerns ancestral joint-family property and a marriage-capable member with a congenital disqualification survives as the sole remaining coparcener under the law applicable to the succession, that member takes the entire estate.

issues.legal_issue: A single judge who disagrees with a governing Full Bench decision must follow the prescribed procedure for obtaining reconsideration rather than refusing to follow or effectively overruling that decision.
material_facts: A Full Bench had previously decided the relevant question of Hindu law.
The single judge declined to follow that Full Bench decision and reached a contrary result.
The single judge did not refer the matter for consideration by a Full Bench or place it before the Chief Justice for a reference.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court deprecated the single judge’s approach and stated that disagreement with a Full Bench decision should be referred to a Full Bench or brought to the Chief Justice for a reference, as required by the applicable practice and rules.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of judicial precedent supports certainty in the law. The Court stated that conventions and rules framed by several High Courts require a single judge or Division Bench that does not agree with a Full Bench decision to make a reference or place the matter before the Chief Justice for that purpose; a judge should not effectively overrule the Full Bench decision. The Court particularly noted the governing Full Bench decisions in Amirthammal v. Vallimayil Ammal, ILR 1942 Mad 807 (FB), and Kesava v. Govindan, ILR 1946 Mad 452 (FB).

rule.if: appeal_from_judgment_disregarding_full_bench_precedent and applicable_full_bench_precedent_exists and single_judge_disagreed_with_precedent and no_reference_procedure_followed

predicates.appeal_from_judgment_disregarding_full_b: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment in which a lower-court judge declined to follow a Full Bench decision.
predicates.applicable_full_bench_precedent_exists: A Full Bench decision governs the legal issue being decided.
predicates.single_judge_disagreed_with_precedent: A single judge reached a conclusion inconsistent with the governing Full Bench decision.
predicates.no_reference_procedure_followed: The judge neither referred the disagreement to a Full Bench nor placed the matter before the Chief Justice for a reference.

issues.definition: When a single judge disagrees with a governing Full Bench decision and has not used the prescribed reference procedure, the judge must seek reconsideration through that procedure rather than disregard the decision.
